questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning the use of antidepressants in eating disorders?

options.text: Medications should not be used as sole treatment for anorexia
Antidepressants act slower in eating disorders than in depression
Antidepressant e�ects are often sustained even after stopping the medications
Antidepressants do not have speci�c antibulimic e�ects
Antidepressants are more e�ective than CBT in anorexia

correct_answer.text: Medications should not be used as sole treatment for anorexia

questions.explanation:
Antidepressants may have some antibulimic e�ects. SSRIs can reduce bingeing rapidly but longer term e�ects are uncertain. In anorexia, the
role of antidepressants is controversial. Medications must not be used as sole treatments in anorexia.

questions.question_text: With respect to epidemiological di�erences between bulimia and anorexia, choose an incorrect statement:

options.text: The prevalence of bulimia is around 2%
Stability of individual diagnoses of various eating disorders is poor.
The prevalence of anorexia is around 0.5% to 1%
Anorexia is excessively represented in lower social classes

correct_answer.text: Anorexia is excessively represented in lower social classes

questions.explanation:
An excess of anorexia was originally observed in higher social class, and this could be due to referral bias. Community studies suggest that
such a class e�ect is indeed absent in current practice.

questions.question_text:
You are considering an antidepressant switch from phenelzine to �uoxetine for a 55-year-old lady with atypical depression. The minimum
washout period required to enable the switching is
questions.explanation:
When switching from phenelzine to �uoxetine, a minimum of 2 weeks gap is advised; when switching from �uoxetine to phenelzine, a
minimum of 5 weeks gap is advised.

questions.question_text:
A 45-year-old man with major depression has been treated with a standard dose of �uoxetine for three months, and he has responded only
partially. He su�ered from severe insomnia and reported it as the most distressing symptom. Which one of the following drugs would you
consider adding at this stage?
questions.explanation: Trazodone has sedative e�ects and could be added to SSRI to treat insomnia that presents as a distressing feature of depression.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old man taking SSRIs developed erectile dysfunction. All of the following are appropriate management options except

options.text: Switch to a di�erent class of antidepressants
Reassure the patient that tolerance will develop in due course
Reduce the dose of antidepressant prescribed

correct_answer.text: Reassure the patient that tolerance will develop in due course

questions.explanation: Tolerance does not develop to sexual side e�ects of SSRIs.

questions.question_text: According to ICD 10, quasi-psychotic episodes with prominent symptoms of anxiety are features of
questions.explanation:
The term 'quasi psychotic episode' is used only for schizotypal disorder in the contemporary classi�catory systems. The ICD10 schizotypal
disorder is characterised by 'occasional transient quasipsychotic episodes with intense illusions, hallucinations and delusion-like ideas
usually occurring without external provocation'. The presence of transient stress-induced paranoid ideations in borderline PD (DSM) is
described as 'micro-psychotic' events.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic feature of avoidant personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
Though people with avoidant personality disorder lack friends, this is not because they prefer loneliness. They are hyper-vigilant to avoid
rejection, but they long for human company, unlike cluster A personality disorders.

questions.question_text: A poor prognostic factor for anorexia nervosa is
questions.explanation:
Though male anorexics tend to have better BMI than females, the prognosis is traditionally considered as worse for male anorectics. Poor
outcome is associated with a strained relationship between a patient and his parents during childhood, the absence of adolescent sexual
behavior and fantasy, long duration of the illness, and greater weight loss during illness.

questions.question_text:
A patient says he is grieving the death of one of his family members who died eight months ago. The assessment indicates he has
symptoms of moderate depression. What would be your next step?
questions.explanation:
This patient had a loss event 8 months ago. He now has symptoms of moderate depression. Bereavement counselling is o�ered to help
coping with loss in an early phase of loss; when diagnosable depression is present, especially after 6 months of loss, treatment for
depression becomes necessary. Denying antidepressants by citing his bereavement is not a useful strategy.

questions.question_text:
A patient known to have bipolar disorder is currently on 500 mg valproate, 20 mg citalopram and 20 mg of olanzapine. He is presently
irritable, tearful and disinhibited. What is the most appropriate thing to do?
questions.explanation:
This is a presentation of mixed a�ective state and must be managed similar to a manic episode. Stop antidepressants as the �rst step and
then consider the optimization of the dose of mood stabilizer.

questions.question_text:
A 21-year-old gentleman was brought to the psychiatric outpatient clinic by his father who was worried about the possible deterioration in
his mental state. On examination, the patient is noted to have auditory hallucinations, and the father had noticed him talking to people who
are not there while he is in his room. He also has a delusional belief that the devil has been tormenting him for many months now. He
remains anxious at home and is progressively isolating himself from everyone. Which of the following is the lifetime prevalence for his
condition (expressed in percentage)?
questions.explanation:
This gentleman probably su�ers from schizophrenia. The life time risk of schizophrenia is about 1%, and the prevalence is approximately the
same in all countries and cultures. The incidence of schizophrenia is about 17-40 per 100,000 population per year.

questions.question_text:
A 19-year-old man with schizophrenia has been treated with an adequate dose of an atypical antipsychotic of his choice for 10 weeks
without much improvement. There are no grounds to suspect treatment nonadherence. The least likely next option for his treatment is
questions.explanation:
There is no place for multiple antipsychotic combination therapies as the same e�ect can be achieved by increasing dose of one drug or by
other methods at a lower side e�ects cost.

questions.question_text:
A 35-year-old woman went to GP surgery one month after the death of her husband. She is tearful, not able to sleep, has a poor appetite
and is pining for her husband. She hears voices of her husband at nighttime and feels his presence. The most appropriate diagnosis is;
questions.explanation:
The stage phase of grief (bereavement) is characterized by acute anguish, which can last for weeks and months. This phase consists of
waves of somatic distress, withdrawal, preoccupation, anger and guilt. (Kaplan and Sadock- Synopsis- pg 67)

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Y is a 27-year-old pregnant lady with a history of low mood and elated mood requiring treatment and is currently euthymic. What is the
risk of her relapse post-partum?
questions.explanation:
The risk of relapse post-partum is 50% in generic bipolar disorder and 50-90% in a patient with a past history of postpartum psychosis. A
signi�cant increase in new psychiatric episodes occurs especially in the �rst 3 months of postpartum period. 80% of these episodes are
mood related (mainly depression).

questions.question_text:
A patient is hospitalised for the treatment of major depressive disorder. What is the chance for development of subsequent episodes of
hypomania/mania?
questions.explanation:
The rate of hypomanic or manic switching in depressed patients without a history of mania or hypomania has been variably estimated as
ranging from 0 -11% to as much as 30% in some smaller uncontrolled studies. In Angst's famous Zurich cohort, 64 of the 908 patients (7.0%)
admitted for depression switched to hypomania or mania. 7-12% is the often quoted proportion in the UK.

questions.question_text:
An anxious father of a 20-year-old man recently diagnosed with schizophrenia asks you about the type of schizophrenia with better
prognosis. Your answer will be
questions.explanation:
The prognostic signi�cance of schizophrenia subtypes employed in ICD-10 and DSM-IV classi�catory systems is controversial. In fact, well-
designed longitudinal studies exploring the prognostic di�erences among the subtypes are scarce. As a result, DSM-5 has removed the
subtypes from its text describing schizophrenia. The paranoid and catatonic subtypes of schizophrenia are supposed to have the best
outcome; disorganised (hebephrenic) subtype has the worst prognosis. The undi�erentiated type has an intermediate prognosis. "Subtyping
and rediagnosis of 187 schizophrenic patients from the Chestnut Lodge follow-up study (19 years long) throws some light into this issue.
Paranoid schizophrenia had an older age at onset, often developed rapidly in individuals with good premorbid functioning, tended to be
intermittent during the �rst 5 years of illness, and was most associated with good outcome or recovery. Hebephrenia had an earlier age at
onset, often developed insidiously, and was associated with a greater family history of psychopathology, poor premorbid functioning, and,
frequently, a continuous illness with a poor long-term prognosis. While also early and insidious in onset, unlike hebephrenia,
undi�erentiated schizophrenia was poorly distinguished from the patients' premorbid state, associated with an early history of behavioral
di�culties, and often resulted in a continuous but stable disability (intermediate between paranoid and hebephrenic)". DSM-IV-TR
guidebook Pg 170 and Fenton, W. S. and McGlashan, T. H. (1991) Natural History of Schizophrenia Subtypes: I. Longitudinal Study of
Paranoid, Hebephrenic, and Undi�erentiated Schizophrenia. Arch Gen Psychiatry, 48, 969-977 (Retrieved from

questions.question_text: The best intervention for acute lithium toxicity with neurological symptoms is
questions.explanation: The most e�ective way of rapid lithium removal is haemodialysis.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Y presents to the medical emergency department with a history of apathy and weight loss. On further investigations, he has
hyponatraemia and hyperkalemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most common symptoms of Addison's disease are fatigue, lightheadedness, muscle weakness, apathy, fever, weight loss, anxiety,
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, sweating, changes in mood and personality, joint and muscle pains. Some have marked cravings for
salt or salty foods due to hyponatraemia. A�ected individuals may note increased tanning since adrenal insu�ciency is manifested in the
skin primarily by hyperpigmentation. Other features include hypoglycemia, low blood pressure, hyperkalemia and hypercalcemia

questions.question_text: Head injury increases the risk of which of the following psychiatric conditions?
questions.explanation:
The largest and methodologically most sound nested case-control study of the association between head injury and psychosis was carried
out by Harrison et al. (2006) using Swedish registers. After head injury exposure, there seems to be a small increase in the risk (OR 1.37) of
non-schizophrenic, non-a�ective psychoses but not schizophrenic disorder (OR 1.10 – not signi�cant). "There was no critical period e�ect for
exposures in early childhood, the association with non-a�ective psychosis being observed only in those exposed to a head injury after age
10. There was no evidence that associations di�ered in males and females or in those with, and those without, a family history of psychosis.
It is unlikely that head injury causes schizophrenia. There is a small but signi�cant risk of non-schizophrenic psychotic disorders, but this is
not associated with early age of injury or family history of psychosis". (Ref: Harrison G et al., "Risk of schizophrenia and other non-a�ective
psychosis among individuals exposed to head injury: Case-control study," Schizophrenia Research 88, no. 1-3 (2006): 119-126: Excerpt
retrieved from

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a prominent risk factor for schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
The greatest risk factor for schizophrenia is having a schizophrenic relative and it is now accepted that 70% of the heritability of
schizophrenia is genetic. The risk increases with (1) the degree of relatedness to the schizophrenic relative (2) if multiple relatives are
a�ected (3) if family members who are a�ected have early onset and/or severe schizophrenic symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mr.Y is a 40 year old gentleman with a long standing history of paranoid schizophrenia. Although he still harbours some chronic delusions of
reference these do not have any signi�cant impact on his functioning as much as the other symptoms. During his presentation to the out-
patient clinic he was noted to be dishevelled, unwashed and his a�ect could be described to be �at. He has no interest in any recreational
activities and spends most of his time sitting in front of the television. Which of the following antipsychotic medications would be most
appropriate to treat his condition?
questions.explanation:
The gentleman is experiencing negative symptoms of schizophrenia characterised by anhedonia, asociality, a�ective �attening and lack of
motivation. Older anti psychotics have only a small e�ect against primary negative symptoms and can cause secondary negative symptoms
(EPSE). Atypical anti psychotics cause, few EPSEs and many trials report statistically signi�cant di�erences in favour of the atypical drugs in
treating negative symptoms. More Robust data support the e�ectiveness of Amisulpride in the treatment of primary negative symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Tom is a 13-year-old boy who smokes cannabis over the last 6 months and his mum is concerned. She asks you by how much this will
increase the chances of him developing schizophrenia? Your answer is
questions.explanation:
The Dunedin cohort study was performed in 1037 adolescents from New Zealand and showed that cannabis consumption at age 15 years
signi�cantly increased the risk of developing schizophrenia (4.5-fold, 95% CI: 1.1 –18.2) up to age 26. How- ever, cannabis consumption at
age 18 increased the risk only 1.7-fold (95% CI: 0.7 –4.2).

questions.question_text: What would you do for a patient with OCD and no improvement after two months on 50mg of sertraline?
questions.explanation:
The dose required to treat OCD is higher than the dose required for depression, and initial response can take 10-12 weeks. (Maudsley.2007).
If there is no response to initial starting doses of SSRIs, the dose should be gradually increased. (NICE.2005) Venlafaxine and valproate are
not indicated at this stage for OCD. Antipsychotics may be used as second line augmenting agents.Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 9th
edition, page 252.NICE Guidelines. Obsessive-compulsive disorder: Core interventions in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder
and body dysmorphic disorder.2005

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with respect to the prognosis of schizophrenia?

options.text: Poor premorbid functioning increases early suicide rates
Female patients have a higher rate of suicide
Presence of mood symptoms has no in�uence on outcome
Prognosis is better in developing countries

correct_answer.text: Prognosis is better in developing countries

questions.explanation:
The better prognosis of patients in developing countries has been well documented [1,2]. For example, a �ve-year follow-up of patients
initially included in the International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia found that clinical and social outcomes were signi�cantly better for
patients in centers in Agra and Ibadan than for those in centers in developed countries

questions.question_text:
When taken as needed, beta blockers such as atenolol can reduce performance anxiety in social phobia. How long before an anticipated
performance should atenolol be taken in order to be e�ective?
questions.explanation: Atenolol must be taken at least an hour before the anticipated performance.

questions.question_text:
A 34-year-old man is being treated for insomnia with hypnotics. His most prominent problem is frequent awakenings through the course of
sleep. He is able fall asleep normally. Which of the following agents is the best choice?
questions.explanation:
Temazepam has a longer half life compared to Z hypnotics which can help prolong the course of sleep troubled by frequent interruptions.
Shorter acting drugs may be more useful as sleep inducers.

questions.question_text:
A 44-year-old man complains of having ejaculation within few seconds of initiating sexual act. He is very embarrassed and seeks treatment.
Which of the following is the best treatment option?
questions.explanation:
SSRIs delay ejaculation and can be used therapeutically. Paroxetine has the best response rate. Sildena�l, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, is
used for erectile dysfunction, not premature ejaculation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation:
SSRIs are associated with an increased risk of hyponatraemia (OR around 3) compared with other classes of antidepressant drugs. Elderly
female patients using diuretics concomitantly with SSRIs are at the highest risk of experiencing hyponatraemia.

questions.question_text: Choose an accurate statement with regard to depression in patients with a terminal illness.

options.text: It does not respond to antidepressants
Depression is uncommon in palliative care settings
somatic symptoms are the most useful in diagnosis

questions.explanation:
SSRIs do not have much evidence but are widely used in depressed patients receiving palliative care. Low dose amitriptyline (avoid in
delirium risk; useful if neuropathic pain), lofepramine and rapid-acting psychostimulant such as dexamphetamine or methylphenidate (in a
patient who has only weeks of life) are other useful options.

questions.question_text: In which of the following anxiety disorders is a beta blocker particularly useful?
questions.explanation:
Speci�c social phobia seen in public speaking or performance can be controlled e�ectively with beta-blocker without causing sedation or
cognitive impairment associated with benzodiazepines.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old lady with bipolar a�ective disorder develops sores in her mouth. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be implicated?
questions.explanation: Sores in the mouth or around the eyes are side e�ects of lamotrigine, which is used for treatment of bipolar depression.

questions.question_text: What is the most characteristic feature expected in a patient with serotonin syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Serotonin syndrome is characterized by Sternbach's triad of altered mental status, neuromuscular abnormalities and autonomic
hyperacticity. Analysis of an extensive series of cases of serotonin toxicity found neuromuscular abnormalities to be the most reliable
diagnostic �nding. Clonus, hyperre�exia, and muscle rigidity nearly always are evident, and shivering may be present. Dunkley EJ, Isbister
GK, Sibbritt D, Dawson AH, Whyte IM. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: simple and accurate diagnostic decision rules for serotonin
toxicity. QJM. 2003;96(9):635-642.

questions.question_text: According to the description in ICD10, patients with schizotypal disorder have

options.text: Duration of symptoms lasting at least 2 years

correct_answer.text: Duration of symptoms lasting at least 2 years

questions.explanation:
Schizotypal disorder is characterized by eccentric behaviour and anomalies of thinking and a�ect which resemble those seen in
schizophrenia, though no de�nite and characteristic schizophrenic anomalies have occurred at any stage. There is no dominant or typical
disturbance, but any of the following may be present: (a) inappropriate or constricted a�ect (the individual appears cold and aloof);); (b)
behaviour or appearance that is odd, eccentric, or peculiar; (c) poor rapport with others and a tendency to social withdrawal; (d) odd beliefs
or magical thinking, in�uencing behaviour and inconsistent with subcultural norms; (e) suspiciousness or paranoid ideas ; (f) obsessive
ruminations without inner resistance, often with dysmorphophobic, sexual or aggressive contents;(g) unusual perceptual experiences
including somatosensory (bodily) or other illusions, depersonalization or derealization; (h) vague, circumstantial, metaphorical,
overelaborate, or stereotyped thinking, manifested by odd speech or in other ways, without gross incoherence;(i) occasional transient quasi-
psychotic episodes with intense illusions, auditory or other hallucinations, and delusion-like ideas, usually occurring without external
provocation. If the term is used, three or four of the typical features listed above should have been present, continuously or episodically, for
at least 2 years.

questions.question_text: Compared to their healthy peers, patients with schizophrenia die how many years earlier in average?
questions.explanation:
Patients with schizophrenia die on average 10 years earlier than their peers without schizophrenia (Tsuang et al in 1980). In addition to
suicide schizophrenic patients are at increased risk of death from accidents and cardiovascular disease, and increased mortality which may
be caused directly or indirectly by the disease or their treatment.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements is incorrect about schizophrenia?

options.text: 10% of women with schizophrenia are �rst diagnosed after 45 years of age
Schizophrenia is more common in immigrants
Schizophrenia is more common in males than females
Schizophrenia is more common in urban areas and in lower social economic classes
Males are diagnosed about 5 years younger (range 15-25 years) than females (range 25-35 years)

correct_answer.text: Schizophrenia is more common in males than females

questions.explanation:
Schizophrenia is equally common in both males and females. According to Drifter hypothesis individuals with schizophrenia become
�nancially dependent because of the steady decline due to their illness and the functional decline associated with schizophrenia drives
schizophrenic and pre-schizophrenic individuals to inner city accommodation. According to Breeder hypothesis, the deprivation and the
stresses of emigration itself increases the risk of developing schizophrenia. The increased frequency of schizophrenia in lower socio-
economic groups, urban dwellers and immigrants may be because deprivation causes schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: A young man started on risperidone presents with sexual side e�ects. Which investigation would you perform now?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone can cause hyperprolactinaemia leading to sexual side e�ects like lack of sexual desire, delayed ejaculation in men and
amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea in women.

questions.question_text:
A 34-year-old inpatient is on clozapine therapy for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has weekly blood count monitoring. In which of the
following situations continuation of clozapine at the same dose is warranted?
questions.explanation:
Red alert from WBC monitoring, new onset diabetic ketoacidosis, myocarditis, amber alert but with clinical features of impaired immunity
are indications to terminate clozapine therapy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications is least a�ected by the variations in CYP2D6 mediated metabolism?
questions.explanation:
Reboxetine is mostly metabolized by CYP3A3/4 metabolism. The important psychotropic substrates of CYP2D6 include typical antipsychotics,
risperidone, tricyclic antidepressants, �uoxetine, paroxetine, venlafaxine, mirtazapine, donepezil and galantamine. In general SSRIs depend
on CYP2C19 system for most of their elimination. Bupropion, moclobemide, mirtazapine, reboxetine, sertraline and citalopram are not
primarily metabolized by the CYP2D6 system

questions.question_text: What is the mechanism behind QT prolongation caused by antipsychotics?

options.text: Increasing number of fast acting sodium channels

questions.explanation:
Prolongation of the QT interval (or QTc interval when corrected for heart rate) results from lengthening of ventricular action potentials. This
can be caused by blockade of potassium channels which are responsible for terminating the plateau phase of the action potential. Although
many potassium channels may produce this e�ect, it is believed that the majority of QT-prolonging drugs block the human ether-a-go-go-
related gene (HERG) ion channel that conducts the rapidly activating delayed recti�er potassium current (IKr). Preclinical testing for drugs in
development now routinely includes assessment of their ability to block HERG and IKr. Finlayson K, Witchel HJ, McCulloch J, et al. Acquired
QT interval prolongation and HERG: implications for drug discovery and development. Eur J Pharmacol 2004;500:129-42

questions.question_text:
A patient has a history of pervasive distrust and suspiciousness regarding his neighbours. Which of the following features will strongly
favour a diagnosis of schizophrenia instead of paranoid personality disorder?

options.text: Continuous, non episodic nature of symptoms

questions.explanation:
Presence of positive symptoms of psychosis is indicative of schizophrenia. Early age of onset and continuous nature of symptoms are likely
to be seen in paranoid personality disorder too. Having episodes of depression and family history of schizophrenia are non speci�c
di�erences and are seen in both conditions.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not an environmental factor known to be associated with an increased risk of schizophrenia?

options.text: Maternal in�uenza in pregnancy and winter births
Complications of pregnancy, delivery and neonatal period

questions.explanation:
Positive family history is a genetic factor and not an environmental factor that is associated with an increased risk of schizophrenia. Genetic
factors account for the majority of liability to schizophrenia and heritability estimates range from 60 to 80%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following classes of drugs can cause peripheral neuropathy as a side e�ect?
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuropathy has been reported as a rare side e�ect of MAOIs like Phenelzine, Isocarboxazid and Tranylcypromine.

questions.question_text:
A 33-year-old man presents with odd eccentric behaviour, social withdrawal and quasi-psychotic episodes with intense illusions. His most
likely diagnosis is;
questions.explanation:
Patients with schizotypal personality disorder (in ICD10 - classi�ed as a type of schizophrenia) usually appear odd or eccentric, may have
illusions, magical thinking, obsessions without resistance, may be members of quasi-cultural groups, with thought disorders and paranoia,
may believe in ESP, clairvoyance etc and may have transient psychotic features.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder varies between  1.9% to 7.9% in the general population. It a�ects males twice
as often as females.  Ref:

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is an accurate description of the evidence for olanzapine as a treatment for schizophrenia?

options.text: Pragmatic trials show lower discontinuation rates for olanzapine than typical antipsychotics
Olanzapine is better than clozapine at reducing suicidal behavior over two years in schizophrenia patients
Olanzapine is better than amisulpiride at reducing psychotic symptoms at two months
Olanzapine is better than standard antipsychotic drugs at reducing psychotic symptoms over six to eight weeks
Olanzapine is associated with fewer extrapyramidal adverse e�ects than standard antipsychotic drugs

correct_answer.text: Olanzapine is associated with fewer extrapyramidal adverse e�ects than standard antipsychotic drugs

questions.explanation:
No signi�cant di�erence has been shown in psychotic symptoms over six to eight weeks between olanzapine and standard antipsychotic
drugs. But olanzapine is associated with fewer extrapyramidal adverse e�ects than standard antipsychotic drugs. InterSePT trial (n=890) of
people with schizophrenia at high risk of suicide, found that clozapine signi�cantly reduced suicidal behavior over two years compared with
Olanzapine. Amisulpiride and olanzapine over two months had no sign�cant di�erence in symptom reduction at two months.

questions.question_text:
A 45-year-old gentleman with bipolar disorder has been taking lithium for many years. He has now developed renal impairment. The
medication of choice would be;
questions.explanation:
No mood stabilizer is clearly preferred to another and avoids lithium. Suggest start one of the following at a low dose and increase slowly,
monitor for adverse e�ects; Valproate, carbamazepine and Lamotrigine. Sodium valproate: Approximately 2% excreted unchanged. Dose
adjustment usually not required in renal impairment

questions.question_text: Night terrors are associated with disturbance in which of the following stages of sleep?
questions.explanation: Night terror is a NREM stage 3-4 disorder.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following �ndings has not been demonstrated in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia?

options.text: Reduced volume in the prefrontal cortex
Reduction in the size of medial temporal lobe structures

questions.explanation:
Neuropathological studies shows that brains from schizophrenic patients weigh less and have larger ventricles than brains from controlled
subjects matched for age and sex. There is also evidence that ventricular enlargement is present at diagnosis and does not progress in
schizophrenic patients. There is a reported reduction in size of mesial temporal lobe structures (hippocampus, parahippocampus and
amygdala) - Bogerts et al (1985). Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated smaller thalamus, hippocampus and superior temporal lobes
bilaterally -Flaun et al (1995)). Basal ganglia enlargement can occur as a result of chronic treatment with typical antipsychotic drugs and this
may be reversed by treatment with Clozapine- Chakos et al (1995).Ref; Core Psychiatry- pg 259-293.

questions.question_text: The most common neurological side e�ect seen when using �uoxetine is
questions.explanation:
Nervous system side e�ects including headache, anxiety, nervousness, insomnia, drowsiness, sedation, tremor, dizziness, jitteriness, and
fatigue have all been reported when taking �uoxetine. The reported incidence of each of these e�ects ranges between 4% and 20% of
treated patients. Among these insomnia is the commonest neurological side e�ect due to �uoxetine, followed by tremors. The tremor
shown by the patients taking �uoxetine is physiological in nature and has a frequency of between 6 and 12 Hz. Placebo can cause headache
as frequently as �uoxetine. Expert Opin Drug Saf. 2004 Sep;3(5):495-504

questions.question_text: The most likely good prognostic factor in schizophrenia in a patient of age 20 is
questions.explanation:
Men get ill with schizophrenia, on average, 4-6 years earlier than women. This is one of the most replicated �ndings in schizophrenia
research. Puzzlingly, however, in schizophrenia that runs in families, there appears to be no onset age di�erence between men and women.
Women recover faster. They stay in hospital for shorter periods and are discharged on a lower antipsychotic dose than their male peers. In
other words, schizophrenic illness, at least at the beginning, interrupts women's lives to a lesser degree than it does men's. After
hospitalization, women return to employment more often than men do; they more often date, marry, and bear children; they develop and
maintain larger and more intimate social support networks (this may be a dimension of better outcome; it is also a preexisting condition that
determines better outcome); and they adhere better to their prescribed treatment regimen than men do. Seeman MV. Current outcome in
schizophrenia: women vs men. Acta Psychiatr Scand. 1986;73:609-617.

questions.question_text: The strongest predictor of mortality in a patient with anorexia nervosa is
questions.explanation: Longitudinal studies have shown that alcohol use is the most dangerous association in terms of mortality in anorexia.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about outcome of schizophrenia is incorrect?

options.text: 8% of patients experience recurrent episodes of illness and develop signi�cant non progressive impairment
35% of schizophrenic patients experience recurrent episodes of illness and have no or slight residual impairment
Social recovery occurs in 1 in 7 patients over a 16-years period after the onset
22% of patients experience a simple episode of acute schizophrenia and have no residual impairment
35% of patients experience recurrent episodes of illness and develop signi�cant progressive impairment

correct_answer.text: Social recovery occurs in 1 in 7 patients over a 16-years period after the onset

questions.explanation:
It is generally accepted that schizophrenia follows one of the 4 courses described above by Shepherd et. al in 1989. In terms of social
recovery Kraepelin in 1919 reported that fewer than 20% of his patients recovered. Mayer-Gross in 1932 working at the same hospital 10
years later reported social recovery in almost 1 in 3 of his patients over a 16 year interval and the results were similar to those of Bleuler in
1978. Ref; Core Psychiatry; pg 259-293

questions.question_text:
A 23-year-old man is diagnosed with schizophrenia. Which of the following is the most common symptom that may be observed in this
man?
questions.explanation:
IPSS study established loss of insight (measured categorically as an all or none phenomenon) as the most common feature seen in around
97% of those with schizophrenia. This was followed by auditory hallucinations (74%). More recent dimensional measurements show that
nearly 60% of patients with schizophrenia lack insight. Report of the International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia. Geneva: World Health
Organisation, 1973.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is sometimes associated with fatal cardiomyopathy when used by patients with bulimia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Ipecac contains emetine, a substance that produces vomiting and can also cause myopathy and cardiac failure.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding induced or shared delusional disorder?

options.text: It is more common in men
It has a good recovery rate
It is more common in children

questions.explanation:
Induced delusional disorders are accepted as a category and exist as F24 in ICD10. It is more common in couples and often involved
nonbizarre delusions. It is more common in women and has a low recovery rate.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medication increases serum lithium levels?
questions.explanation:
Indomethacin is a Non steroidal anti-in�ammatory drug, which inhibits the release of renal prostaglandins, thereby reducing renal blood
�ow and possibly increasing renal absorption of sodium and therefore Lithium. (Maudlsey guidelines- Pg 132)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about lithium is true?

options.text: Polyuria occurs mainly with once daily dosing
Lithium causes more weight gain than sodium valpraote
Lithium increase the risk of hypoparathyroidism
20% of middle aged women develop hypothyroidism

correct_answer.text: 20% of middle aged women develop hypothyroidism

questions.explanation:
In the longer term, lithium increases the risk of hypothyroidism. In middle-aged women, the risk may be up to 20%. Hypothyroidism is easily
treated with thyroxine. Lithium also increases the risk of hyperparathyroidism and some recommend calcium levels should be monitored for
patients on long-term treatment. Polyuria occurs mainly with twice daily dosing. Mean weight gain is higher with valproate than lithium in
many studies, atleast in the �rst 12 weeks after initiation.

questions.question_text: In terms of changes seen in the sleep architecture of older people, which of the following statements is incongruent?

options.text: More slow wave sleep and REM sleep

correct_answer.text: More slow wave sleep and REM sleep

questions.explanation:
In old age, an absolute reduction occurs in both slow-wave sleep and REM sleep. An increase in the frequency of awakenings after sleep
onset also occurs with increasing age.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct about people with dual role transvestism?

options.text: The individual has a desire to live and be accepted as a member of the opposite sex
Cross dressing results in sexual arousal and grati�cation
There is sexual motivation for the cross dressing
The individual has desire for a permanent change to the opposite sex.
The individual experiences a sense of appropriateness by wearing clothes of the other gender

correct_answer.text: The individual experiences a sense of appropriateness by wearing clothes of the other gender

questions.explanation:
In dual role transvestism, the individual wears clothes of the opposite sex in order to experience temporary membership in the opposite
sex. The individual experiences a sense of appropriateness by wearing clothes of the other gender. There is no sexual motivation for the
cross-dressing. The individual has no desire for a permanent change to the opposite sex. This must be di�erentiated from fetishistic
transvestism where cross-dressing results in sexual arousal often associated with masturbation or sexual activity. This is classi�ed as a
paraphilia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has been found consistently in clinical trials to reduce the negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
In a review of the best available evidence on drug treatments for schizophrenia, Nadeem et al. concluded that no intervention has been
found to reduce negative symptoms consistently. Nadeem Z, McIntosh A, Lawrie S (2003) Schizophrenia. Clin Evid 2003: 1208, 1237.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime risk of developing schizophrenia for a child born to a patient with schizophrenia, if the other parent is healthy?
questions.explanation:
If the other parent of the child also has, schizophrenia then the lifetime risk for the child is increased to 46%. The lifetime risk of
schizophrenia in the monozygotic twin sibling of the patient is increased to 48% and dizygotic twin sibling of a patient is 17%. The lifetime
risk for the sibling of a schizophrenic patient is 9%.

questions.question_text: Hoover's test is a type of physical examination done to identify the possible diagnosis of
questions.explanation:
Hoover's test is useful to identify patients with conversion disorder, who has paralysis with One or more limbs or one side of the face or
body may be a�ected. Here the patient is unable to raise the a�ected limb from the couch but is able to raise the una�ected limb against
resistance with demonstrable pressing down of the heel on the a�ected side. Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 746

questions.question_text:
A 33 year old lady had two previous episodes of documented hypomania with one episode of depression. She is interested in treatments
that can prevent relapses. Which of the following is least likely to be bene�cial?
questions.explanation:
For a patient with bipolar disorder, there is no evidence that psychoanalysis can prevent relapses. All other listed options have proven
evidence in relapse prevention.

questions.question_text: What would be the probable diagnosis of a person complaining of feeling on the edge all the time?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine is associated with tremors; it can be higher with higher dose.

questions.question_text:
A 22 year old man presents with anxiety that his genitals are misshapen. He is not convinced in spite of plastic surgeon reassuring him by
showing multiple images of normal genital appearances. Which of the following interventions has evidence-based support in the above
situation?
questions.explanation:
Fluoxetine has the best evidence for body Dysmorphophobia. In a triple blinded RCT comparing e�cacy of �uoxetine in body dysmorphic
disorder (40% patients had delusional BDD), �uoxetine was increased by 20 mg/day every 10 days to a maximum of 80 mg/day. Signi�cant
response started occurring at 8 weeks until 12 weeks when the observation was made. Patients who were delusional at baseline were as
likely as non-delusional patients to respond to �uoxetine. Phillips KA, Albertini RS, Rasmussen SA.A randomized placebo-controlled trial of
�uoxetine in body dysmorphic disorder.Arch Gen Psychiatry 2002 Apr;59:381-8

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the most likely option regarding non-pharmacological management of schizophrenia?

options.text: Intensive hostel care improves self care and community skills
Institutionalization of chronically ill patients improves social functioning
Intensive case management is more e�ective than standard care
Occupational therapy decreases social withdrawal and negative symptoms

correct_answer.text: Occupational therapy decreases social withdrawal and negative symptoms

questions.explanation:
Findings suggest that occupational therapy activities decrease negative symptoms of schizophrenia such as �at a�ect, mutism, apathy,
dissocial, loss of attention.

questions.question_text: All of the following are predictors of worse outcome in PTSD except

options.text: Higher degree of numbing after trauma

questions.explanation: Females have worse outcome for PTSD than males.

questions.question_text: Which medication is more likely to exacerbate psoriasis?
questions.explanation: Exacerbation of acne and psoriasis is associated with Lithium therapy

questions.question_text: Which of the following features observed during trauma has the capacity to predict future development of PTSD?
questions.explanation:
Emotional numbing during trauma has been reported to predict future PTSD. Similarly dissociative experiences during trauma may also
predict PTSD later on.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is employed as a screening tool in clinical psychiatry?
questions.explanation:
Edinburgh Postnatal depression scale is a quick screening tool that can be used by midwives and nurses to identify depression in pregnant
mothers ante/post partum.

questions.question_text: According to DSM-5 criteria which of the following features must be present before a diagnosis of neuroleptic malignant syndrome is made?

options.text: High creatinine kinase up to 300 micrograms and rigidity

questions.explanation:
DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for NMS: Exposure to dopamine antagonsit in the last 72 hours, along with severe muscle rigidity and elevated
temperature as well as mental status alteration (reduced or �uctuating level of consciousness), CK elevation (at least 4 times upper limit of
normal), sympathetic nervous system lability, de�ned as at least 2 of the following:(hypertension, >25% of baseline, blood pressure
�uctuation of =20 mmHg diastolic or =25 mmHg systolic change within 24 hours, diaphoresis, urinary incontinence), hypermetabolism,
de�ned as heart rate increase (=25% above baseline) and respiratory rate increase (=50% above baseline). These features must be present
along with a negative work-up for infectious, toxic, metabolic, and neurological causes. practice/monograph/990/diagnosis/criteria.html

questions.question_text: A young man in your clinic complains of EPSEs. The scale you would use to measure this is:
questions.explanation:
A number of general scales have been developed for extrapyramidal symptoms which incorporate items for rating drug-induced
Parkinsonism. These include Chouinard et al's Extrapyramidal Rating Scale (Chouinard et al, 1980), the Targeting Abnormal Kinetic E�ects
(TAKE) scale (Wojcik et al, 1980), the Extrapyramidal Symptoms Scale (Adler et al, 1989) and the Neurological Rating Scale for Extrapyramidal
E�ects (Simpson-Angus scale; Simpson and Angus, 1970). The scales vary in the emphasis they place on the di�erent features of drug-
induced parkinsonism. The TAKE scale, places more emphasis on akinesia and bradykinesia while the Simpson-Angus scale places the
majority of emphasis on rigidity. The choice of scale may vary according to the purposes of the clinician or investigator, but the Simpson-
Angus scale, which was the �rst to be developed, remains the most widely used.Excerpted from Gervin and Barnes. Assessment of drug-
related movement disorders in schizophrenia. Advan. Psychiatr. Treat., Sep 2000; 6: 332 - 341.

questions.question_text:
Mr.X is a 36-year-old gentleman who has a long-standing diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He still remains psychotic despite trying him
on a trial of various antipsychotics including Haloperidol, Olanzapine and Risperidone. You would like to consider him for a trial of
Clozapine. Which one among the following investigations should be ordered on this patient before starting Clozapine?
questions.explanation:
Clozapine is an atypical anti psychotic drug which is mainly used for the treatment of resistant schizophrenia. Around 2.7% of patients
treated with Clozapine develop neutropenia. Of these, half do so within the �rst 18 weeks of treatment and 3/4 by the end of the �rst year.
Risk factors include: Black Afro-Caribbean (77% increased risk) and young and having a low base rate white cell count. At least 0.7%
Clozapine treated patients develop agranulocytosis which is potentially fatal.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drug is a recognised cause of depression?
questions.explanation:
Clonidine is an alpha2 adrenoreceptor agonist. Depression is uncommon but recognised side e�ect of clonidine, and usually presents when
the drug is initially introduced. Its prevalence is about 1 % Houton, M.C. Clonidine hydrochloride: review of pharmacologic and clinical
aspects. Prog Cardiovasc Dis 1981, 23: 337-350.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychotropics signi�cantly interfere with oral contraceptives?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine induces the metabolism of OCPs leading to contraception failure.

questions.question_text:
Depression rating scales may overlap with negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Which of the following rating scales is speci�c for
measuring symptoms of depression in those with schizophrenia?

options.text: Centre for epidemiological studies depression scale (CES-D)

questions.explanation:
Calgary depression scale was speci�cally developed to avoid measurement redundancy with negative symptoms while evaluating
depression in schizophrenia patients. CES-D is a tool to measure depression in community samples.

questions.question_text:
A patient with bipolar disorder is already maintained on quetiapine but experiences a manic episode. What drug would you use to treat the
current episode of mania?
questions.explanation:
Both BAP guidelines and NICE bipolar guidelines endorse the use of add-on lithium or valproate when acute mania occurs despite being
treated with antipsychotic for maintenance. Though there is little to separate between lithium and valproate in terms of the
recommendations in this situation, BAP suggests valproate may be better suited in acute episodes of mania due to dosing �exibility.

questions.question_text: The risk of suicide one year after an act of self-harm is
questions.explanation:
Between 40% and 60% of people who die by suicide have a history of at least one episode of DSH. In a 15-year follow-up data analysed at
Oxford Monitoring System for self-harm, the suicide risk in the �rst year following DSH was 0.7% (66 times the general population risk). The
risk was higher in males (1.1%) than females (0.5%), although the excess risk compared with suicide risk in the general population was
greater in females (90 times) than males (64 times). By the end of 15 years of follow-up, suicide had occurred in 4.8% of males and 1.8% of
females. The risk of suicide continued throughout 15 years of follow-up. The risk of suicide was signi�cantly greater in the �rst year following
DSH in those patients who were repeaters of DSH at their �rst presentation in the study period (1.1%) compared with those for whom this
presentation was the �rst ever episode of DSH (0.6%). Hawton, K., Zahl, D., Weatherall, R. (2003) Suicide following deliberate self-harm: long-
term follow-up of patients who presented to a general hospital. British Journal of Psychiatry, 182, 537-542.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with an increase in impulsivity in patients with borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are associated with an increase in impulsivity in borderline patients.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated during breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
Atypical antipsychotic: Limited data suggests sulpride; olanzapine and risperidone are safe in breast feeding. However, a decision to
continue needs to be done on individual risk/bene�ts analysis. There are no published data on Aripiprazole, Amisulpride, Sertindole and
Ziprasidone. Clozapine is contraindicated during breast-feeding as it accumulates in breast milk and foetal serum. A Higher concentration of
clozapine is due to a higher concentration of albumin in the foetal blood. Reported adverse e�ects- Agranulocytosis ( but recovered
spontaneously after discontinuation), decreased sucking re�ex, drowsiness seizure, irritability and cardiovascular instability.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs would be the most e�ective treatment for a 38-year- old man with acute mania?
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics or sodium valproate should be used the �rst line in the treatment of acute mania because of their rapid antimanic e�ect.

questions.question_text:
A 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa was transferred from an eating disorder unit to a medical emergency unit after
losing consciousness. On admission, she appeared extremely emaciated,with low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema. Which of the
following complications of anorexia is the most likely explaantion for her presentation?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, pulmonary embolism is rarely a direct complication of anorexia. First-degree heart block, though common in
anorexia, is not symptomatic on its own. Sinus bradycardia, not tachycardia, is noted in anorexia; patients can have prolonged QTc and the
resultant risk of torsades de pointes. The most likely explanation is an underlying cardiomyopathy (due to starvation in restricting type of
AN) with sudden decompensation leading to cardiac failure. Another common cardiac abnormality is mitral valve prolapse, which often
remits with weight gain. Clinically important mitral valve regurgitation is, however, exceedingly infrequent. Pneumothorax is extremely rare,
but pneumomediastinum/pneumothorax can occur as a complication of anorexia. Rome, E. S. and Ammerman, S. (2003) Medical
complications of eating disorders: an update. Journal of Adolescent Health, 33, 418-426

questions.question_text:
A 33-year-old man with history of schizophrenia has moderately severe renal failure. Which of the following drugs undergoes signi�cant
renal excretion?
questions.explanation:
Amisulpride is primarily renally excreted. 50% of the consumed drug is excreted unchanged in urine. It is not recommended when the GFR is
less than 10ml/min, so it is best avoided in established renal failure. Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 10th edition- Pg 369

questions.question_text:
You are seeing a patient with chronic schizophrenia who has always complained of dry mouth. Which of the following antipsychotic drug is
least likely to cause this adverse e�ect?
questions.explanation: Amisulpride is least likely to cause dryness of mouth and is an ideal choice.

questions.question_text: A�ective dysregulation is the principal psychopathology of which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
A�ective dysregulation refers to the instability of a�ect resulting from dysfunction of emotion regulation system. It is the core de�cit in
bipolar spectrum disorders and borderline personality.

questions.question_text: The most commonly observed speci�c catatonic phenomenon in those with a diagnosis of schizophrenia is
questions.explanation:
According to Abrams and Taylor (1976), mannerisms are the most common, followed, in descending order of frequency, by stereotypies,
stupor, negativism, automatism and echopraxia

questions.question_text: The proportion of patients diagnosed with schizophrenia that experience recurrent relapse and continued disability is
questions.explanation:
About three-quarters of people experience recurrent relapse and continued disability, although the proportion of people who improved
signi�cantly increased after the mid-1950s. Nadeem Z, McIntosh A, Lawrie S (2003) Schizophrenia. Clin Evid 2003: 1208, 1237.

questions.question_text:
Which one of the following best re�ects the evidence on the adverse e�ects of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) when used in the treatment
of moderate to severe depression?

options.text: Simulated ECT causes same degree of memory loss as ECT immediately after treatment
Bilateral ECT is more likely to cause transient memory loss than unilateral ECT
ECT is more likely to cause memory loss six months after treatment than simulated ECT
Low dose ECT is more likely to cause transient memory loss than high dose ECT
ECT causes no direct damage to memory in non-depressed individuals

correct_answer.text: Bilateral ECT is more likely to cause transient memory loss than unilateral ECT

questions.explanation:
A systematic review has concluded that (1) bilateral ECT is more likely to cause transient memory loss than unilateral ECT; (2) ECT is more
likely to cause transient memory loss immediately after treatment than simulated ECT, but there is no signi�cant di�erence in cognitive
functioning at six months; (3) High dose ECT was more likely to cause transient memory loss than low dose ECT. UK ECT Review Group (2003)
E�cacy and safety of electroconvulsive therapy in depressive disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet 361: 799, 808
